title: 30 by 30

definition.text: A global initiative for governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean area by 2030.

facts.text: It was proposed in a 2019 Science Advances article, 'A Global Deal for Nature', partly to help mitigate climate change.
Launched by the High Ambition Coalition in 2020, it had more than 100 supporting countries by October 2022.
In December 2022 it became Target 3 of the 23 targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
As of May 2026, 17.3% of land and inland waters and 9.8% of marine areas were protected; counting OECMs, 18.4% and 10.0%.
Some conservationists say the 30% figure lacks clear scientific justification, while others argue it is too low and point to the Half-Earth idea of conserving about 50%.
Critics warn that broad definitions counting OECMs with intensive industrial activity could inflate reported progress.
NGOs and Indigenous groups warn it could lead to forced evictions, 'green grabbing' and green colonialism without human-rights safeguards.

contested_note: Researchers dispute whether 30% is scientifically justified, too low, or a risk to Indigenous land rights.

definition.text: Protected areas that exist in law but lack the funding, staff or enforcement to stop poaching, logging or development inside them.

facts.text: Modelling suggests that for exploited species, better enforcement in existing reserves often helps more than expanding area without more resources.
Where threats such as over-harvesting are intense, spending on compliance and management can beat creating new, weakly managed reserves.
Where pressures cluster near reserve edges, enlarging protected areas can create secure core refuges even without more staff.
Meeting percentage targets without governance capacity risks spreading scarce conservation money too thin.

definition.text: The European Commission's 2020 plan for biodiversity, offered as the EU's contribution to the post-2020 global framework.

facts.text: It plans to make 30% of EU territory protected by 2030, with 10% strictly protected.
It proposed binding nature restoration targets and is a core part of the European Green Deal.
As of 2023 the EU was not on track to meet its targets.

definition.text: A 2010 supplementary agreement to the Biodiversity Convention on access to genetic resources and fair sharing of the benefits from their use.

facts.text: It implements the CBD's third objective, the fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.
Adopted on 29 October 2010 in Nagoya, Japan, it entered into force on 12 October 2014; by August 2025 it had 142 parties.
It gives each country sovereign rights over its biological resources, making biopiracy illegal.
Access requires prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms; benefits may be monetary or non-monetary, such as royalties or shared research results.
It also covers traditional knowledge linked to genetic resources, which cannot be accessed without permission from the communities holding it.
Users must monitor genetic resources after they leave a country through checkpoints along the value chain, from research to commercialisation.
Marine genetic resources from the high seas fall outside its benefit-sharing regime, because it covers only national jurisdiction.

title: Criticism of the Nagoya Protocol

definition.text: Concerns that the Nagoya Protocol's bureaucracy harms biodiversity research, conservation and disease response.

facts.text: Some developing countries have refused permits for basic biodiversity research and even prosecuted scientists.
Its bilateral transfer system has low throughput, whereas the plant genetic resources treaty's multilateral system allows 8500 transfers every week.
Lack of national implementation is often blamed for the protocol's failure.

related: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
contested_note: Scientists and museums see the protocol as red tape, while providers of genetic resources defend it as protection against biopiracy.
